title: ⚡ Grammar Range & Accuracy

sections.heading: What examiners look for
sections.body: The GRA (Grammatical Range and Accuracy) criterion is 25% of your Writing and Speaking score. It's not just about being error-free — it's about using a VARIETY of structures.

sections.heading: The progression
sections.body:
Band 6: Uses mostly simple sentences with some complex ones. Errors are common.
Band 7: Uses complex sentences with some errors in complex structures.
Band 8: Uses a wide range of structures. Errors are rare.
Band 9: Full range of structures with natural, consistent accuracy.

highlight: You don't need perfect grammar. You need RANGE. Show the examiner you CAN use complex structures.

example.wrong: Technology is good. It helps people. But it has problems too. These problems are many.
example.right: Although technology has undeniably improved quality of life, the challenges it introduces — particularly regarding privacy and social isolation — demand equally thoughtful solutions.

title: 🔗 Complex Sentences: The Foundation
body:
A complex sentence has a MAIN clause + a SUBORDINATE clause connected by a subordinating conjunction.

Think of it like this:
Main clause = can stand alone ✅
Subordinate clause = cannot stand alone ❌

Example:
"Although technology is useful (sub.) ← , it creates problems." (main) ✅
"Although technology is useful." ← WRONG — incomplete thought ❌

quick.label: Cause: because, since, as, given that
Time: when, after, before, once, until

question: Which is a correctly formed complex sentence?
options: Although technology is useful, it creates challenges.
Although, technology is useful. It creates challenges.
Technology is useful although, it creates challenges.
Although technology. It is useful and creates challenges.
correct: Although technology is useful, it creates challenges.
explanation:
✅ Correct structure: Subordinate clause (Although + S + V) + comma + Main clause

❌ Option B: Never put a comma directly after "Although"
❌ Option C: The comma belongs BEFORE "although" only when the main clause comes FIRST
❌ Option D: "Although technology" has no verb — it's not a clause

Rule: When the subordinate clause comes FIRST, put a comma after it. When it comes SECOND, no comma needed.
hint: The subordinate clause with "Although" must have a subject and verb.

sentence: _____ the government invested in education, literacy rates would improve significantly.
explanation:
"If" introduces a condition (first or second conditional).

"Although" = contrast, "Because" = cause/reason, "Whereas" = comparison.

This sentence structure is: If + [condition], [result] — a basic first/second conditional.
hint: This sentence shows a condition and a result — which word introduces conditions?

title: 🔄 Passive Voice in Academic Writing

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.body:
Passive voice makes academic writing more objective and formal. Use it when:
• The doer is unknown or unimportant
• You want to emphasise the action/result
• Standard academic convention requires it

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body:
Active:  Subject + verb + object
"Researchers conducted the study."

Passive: Object + be + past participle [+ by + agent]
"The study was conducted [by researchers]."

sections.heading: Tense forms
sections.body:
Present: is/are + pp → "Data is collected daily"
Past: was/were + pp → "The experiment was conducted"
Perfect: has/have been + pp → "Results have been published"

highlight: In IELTS Task 1 (describing graphs), passive voice is very natural: "A sharp increase was recorded in 2020."

example.wrong: We can see that the researchers found interesting results in the data.
example.right: Notably, the findings reveal a statistically significant correlation — a result that has since been substantiated by three independent studies.

instruction: Rearrange to form a correct passive sentence:
correct: The environment has been significantly damaged by human activity.
explanation:
Structure: The environment (subject) + has been (present perfect passive) + significantly (adverb) + damaged (past participle) + by human activity (agent phrase).

Note: "significantly" goes AFTER "been" and BEFORE "damaged" — adverbs in passive sentences go between the auxiliary and the past participle.

title: 🎯 Conditionals: The Four Types
body:
Type 0 — Always true: "If you heat water to 100°C, it boils."
Type 1 — Real future: "If temperatures rise, sea levels will increase."
Type 2 — Hypothetical present: "If governments invested more, outcomes would improve."
Type 3 — Hypothetical past: "If action had been taken sooner, the crisis could have been avoided."

quick.label: Type 3: If + past perfect → would have + pp

question: Which sentence is a correctly formed SECOND conditional?
options: If the government will invest in renewables, emissions will fall.
If the government invested in renewables, emissions would fall.
If the government had invested in renewables, emissions would fall.
If the government invests in renewables, emissions fall.
correct: If the government invested in renewables, emissions would fall.
explanation:
✅ Second conditional: If + PAST SIMPLE (invested) + comma + would + INFINITIVE (fall)

This expresses a hypothetical or unlikely present/future situation.

❌ Option A uses "will" in both clauses — this would be first conditional but is grammatically wrong
❌ Option C uses "had invested" — this is third conditional (hypothetical past)
❌ Option D is zero conditional (always true facts)
hint: Second conditional: If + past simple... would + bare infinitive.

title: ✏️ Find the Grammar Error
instruction: Identify the sentence that contains a grammatical mistake:

sentences.text: Despite the challenges, the project was completed on time.
Despite of the challenges, the project was completed on time.
sentences.explanation:
"Despite" NEVER takes "of".

✅ Correct: "Despite the challenges..."
✅ Or: "In spite of the challenges..."

"Despite of" is one of the most common errors in IELTS Band 6–7 essays. Memorise: DESPITE + noun/noun phrase. IN SPITE OF + noun/noun phrase.

sentences.text: Although the project faced setbacks, it was completed successfully.
Provided that funding is secured, the project will proceed.

instruction: Match each sentence beginning to the correct ending:

pairs.word: Were the government to invest more,
Not only does social media connect people,

pairs.meaning: I firmly believe action must be taken.

explanation:
These are all sophisticated sentence starters:
• "Although..." = concessive clause (contrast)
• "Were the government to..." = formal conditional inversion (Band 8+)
• "Not only does..." = negative inversion (Band 8+)
• "Having considered..." = perfect participle clause (Band 8+)

question: Which sentence uses INVERSION correctly for emphasis?
options: I have never seen such remarkable progress.
Never I have seen such remarkable progress.
Never have I seen such remarkable progress.
Have never I seen such remarkable progress.
correct: Never have I seen such remarkable progress.
explanation:
✅ Inversion after negative adverbs: NEVER + AUXILIARY (have) + SUBJECT (I) + MAIN VERB (seen)

Inversion is triggered by negative adverbs at the START of a sentence: Never, Rarely, Seldom, Hardly, No sooner, Not only, Under no circumstances.

This is a Band 8–9 structure — using it correctly shows the examiner your grammatical range.
hint: After "Never" at the start of a sentence, flip the auxiliary and subject.
